title: Understand the process of slaughtering farm animals

lessons.title: Before slaughter: law, welfare and preparation
lessons.html:
Before slaughter: law, welfare and preparation

Meat comes from animals slaughtered in a careful, clean and humane way. In South Africa, the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 says that animals slaughtered for meat to be sold must be slaughtered at a registered abattoir, where meat is inspected. This protects people from diseases and unsafe meat. Slaughter for your own household or for cultural and religious ceremonies has its own rules; ask the local state veterinarian or animal health officer what applies.

Why animal welfare matters

The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty a crime. Animals must be handled calmly and killed without unnecessary pain or fear. Stressed animals also give poorer meat: dark, tough meat that spoils faster, and bruises that must be cut away.

Selecting animals for slaughter

  • Only healthy animals may be sent for slaughter. Sick animals must be reported.
  • Check animal treatment records. An animal that was treated with a medicine must not be slaughtered until the withdrawal period on the label or from the vet has passed.
  • Choose animals that meet the buyer's mass and condition requirements.

Preparing animals

  1. Animals are usually kept off feed for some hours before slaughter, as the abattoir instructs, but they must always have water.
  2. Move and load them calmly (see handling and moving animals).
  3. Do not mix strange groups or put horned and hornless animals together on the truck.
  4. At the abattoir, animals rest in lairage pens with water before slaughter. An inspector checks them alive (ante-mortem inspection).

Animals that are sick, injured or not fit are separated and dealt with by the inspector or vet.

lessons.title: The steps of slaughter and meat hygiene
lessons.html:
The steps of slaughter and meat hygiene

At an abattoir trained workers do each step. This lesson explains the process so you understand it; it does not train you to slaughter.

Main steps

  1. Stunning: the animal is made unconscious so it feels no pain, for example with a captive bolt gun or electrical stunning. Stunning must be done correctly the first time.
  2. Bleeding (sticking): the main blood vessels in the neck are cut quickly after stunning so the animal dies from loss of blood while unconscious.
  3. Skinning or scalding: cattle and sheep are skinned. Pigs are usually scalded in hot water and the hair is scraped off.
  4. Evisceration: the stomach, intestines and other organs are removed carefully so the contents do not spill on the meat.
  5. Inspection (post-mortem): a meat inspector checks the carcass and organs for disease. Unsafe parts or whole carcasses are condemned and destroyed.
  6. Splitting, washing and grading: the carcass is split, trimmed and classified (for example by age and fat).
  7. Chilling: carcasses go to the cold room quickly to stop germs growing.

Hygiene

  • Wash hands and sterilise knives in hot water between carcasses.
  • Wear clean protective clothing, boots, hairnet and apron.
  • Keep the clean area (meat) apart from the dirty area (skins, stomachs, live animals).
  • Never let a carcass touch the floor.

Safety

  • Knives: cut away from your body; wear a chain-mail glove or apron where provided.
  • Floors are wet and slippery; wear non-slip boots.
  • Stunning equipment is dangerous; only trained people may use it.
  • Some diseases pass from animals to people. Report sick animals and never open the carcass of an animal that died suddenly; anthrax is a risk.

By-products

Skins, hides, wool, offal and bones are also used. Condemned material is disposed of as the law requires.

Key points

  • Meat for sale must come from a registered abattoir under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000.
  • Only healthy animals past any withdrawal period may be slaughtered.
  • Handle animals calmly; give water before slaughter.
  • Steps: stunning, bleeding, skinning or scalding, evisceration, inspection, chilling.
  • Strict hygiene and safe knife use protect the meat and the workers.
